direct_answer:
Aker BP states it has a zero-tolerance approach to corruption and bribery, implemented through its code of conduct and an anti-corruption policy that applies to all employees and business partners, with mandatory regular anti-corruption/ethics training for staff and an annual code of conduct refresher course for the workforce, executive management and the board [Source 1][Source 3][Source 9][Source 2]. The compliance department oversees corruption/bribery risk, performs an annual compliance risk assessment to identify high-risk areas (including corruption and bribery), develops a tailored compliance training plan (including onboarding training for new employees and non-employees), and reports quarterly to the executive management team and the audit and risk committee [Source 3][Source 9]. Aker BP also has a “speaking up” policy and integrity reporting channels; it ran awareness initiatives and provided training for managers on handling integrity/whistleblowing reports, and received 21 whistleblowing cases via the integrity channel and direct reports to the compliance department in 2024 [Source 1][Source 15][Source 12].

For the reporting period (2024), Aker BP reports no reported incidents of corruption and no convictions or fines for violations of anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws; it also states it has not been convicted of violating corruption and bribery laws [Source 2][Source 1]. The retrieved passages do not describe any public legal proceedings/cases related to corruption during the period beyond these statements, so whether any proceedings occurred (without conviction/fine) cannot be confirmed from the provided evidence [Source 1][Source 2].
compliance_rationale: The passages provide evidence of key elements of an anti-corruption system (policies, risk assessment, training, speaking up mechanisms, and reporting to governance bodies) and quantitative statements on incidents/convictions/fines for 2024 [Source 3][Source 9][Source 1][Source 2]. However, the evidence does not cover several ESRS G1-3/G1-1 specifics (e.g., independence of investigators, detailed procedures for investigation/response, training coverage for functions-at-risk, and details on legal proceedings), limiting full ESRS alignment.
disclosure_gaps: Procedures to detect, investigate, and respond to corruption/bribery allegations/incidents in sufficient detail (e.g., steps, timelines, remediation/actions) are not described in the retrieved passages [Source 3][Source 1].
Whether investigators/investigating committee are separate from the management chain involved is not disclosed [Source 3].
Process for reporting investigation outcomes to administrative/management/supervisory bodies beyond quarterly risk reporting is not specified [Source 3].

How policies are communicated to ensure accessibility/understanding is only described at a high level; no detail on communication methods/coverage for relevant persons (e.g., business partners) [Source 3].

Training details required by ESRS (nature/scope/depth by audience; percentage of functions-at-risk covered; frequency beyond annual refresher; extent of training for administrative/management/supervisory bodies) are incomplete—only completion rates for workforce/board and examples of role-based training are provided [Source 2][Source 7][Source 9].
Functions most at risk regarding corruption and bribery are not explicitly identified (only that some positions are higher risk and that training is tailored) [Source 9].
Confirmed incidents disclosure lacks detail on actions taken to address breaches (even if zero incidents, ESRS G1-4(b) expects actions taken where breaches occur; none are described) [Source 2].

Public legal cases/proceedings related to corruption/bribery (including cases initiated in prior years with outcomes in 2024) are not disclosed; only convictions/fines are addressed [Source 2][Source 1].
key_findings: Zero-tolerance stance supported by code of conduct and an anti-corruption policy applicable to employees and business partners [Source 1][Source 3].

Compliance department oversees corruption/bribery risk, conducts annual compliance risk assessment, and reports quarterly to executive management and the audit and risk committee [Source 3][Source 9].

Mandatory training includes regular anti-corruption/ethics training and an annual code of conduct refresher; 2024 completion: 93% of workforce and 100% of board members [Source 1][Source 2][Source 9].

Speaking up policy and integrity reporting channels are in place; 21 whistleblowing cases received in 2024; manager training and awareness campaigns on speaking up were conducted [Source 1][Source 12][Source 15].

2024: no reported incidents of corruption and no convictions or fines for anti-corruption/anti-bribery law violations; also stated not convicted of violating corruption and bribery laws [Source 2][Source 1].
